newsitem.title: USA: S&P AFFIRMS UNITED GUARANTY RESIDENTIAL INSURANCE.
newsitem.headline: S&P AFFIRMS UNITED GUARANTY RESIDENTIAL INSURANCE.

text.p: NEW YORK, June 30 - Standard & Poor's today has affirmed its triple-'A' issuer credit and claims-paying ability ratings of United Guaranty Residential Insurance Co.

United Guaranty Residential Insurance is primarily an insurer of good, 'A'-quality U.S. residential mortgages eligible for inclusion in mortgage pools guaranteed by the Federal National Mortgage Association and the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. (together, the "government-sponsored enterprises").
The affirmation is based on the following rating factors:

-- Strategic importance to ultimate parent: Standard & Poor's believes that United Guaranty Residential Insurance is strategically important to American International Group Inc. (AIG; triple-'A' issuer credit rating), its ultimate parent company.

-- Strong earnings. Earnings are strong and were up substantially in 1996, continuing a trend of strength and growth that stretches back to 1991. Earnings are broadly representative of those generated by the mortgage insurance industry during this period.

-- Very strong reinsurance protection: United Guaranty Residential Insurance benefits from an aggregate excess-of-loss reinsurance treaty from National Union Fire Insurance Co. of Pittsburgh, Pa. (triple-'A' claims-paying ability rating, AIG's principal domestic property-casualty operating unit). This contract provides very substantial catastrophic risk protection.

-- Conservative, experienced, and successful management. Management has been in place for a considerable length of time and has experienced both good and bad times in the industry. It emphasizes competition based on customer service instead of price cutting.

-- Superior capital, although primary capital position is moderately leveraged. Not taking into account its reinsurance protection, United Guaranty Residential Insurance is the most leveraged of all the mortgage insurers. However, the addition of reinsurance places its capital position near the top of the industry.
-- Good underwriting, loss mitigation and sophisticated risk management techniques. The company's ACCUSCORE underwriting system is comprehensive and sophisticated.

-- Good book of conforming business. Since the beginning of the decade, the business eligible for inclusion in mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by the "government-sponsored enterprises," which constitutes the great majority of the risk written and is known as "conforming" product, has performed well.
United Guaranty Residential Insurance has experienced some worsening of performance of the post-1993 books, but these books are still developing well by historical standards.
-- Good expense control. At 23.7%, the expense ratio is at its best level ever, comparing favorably with the industry.
-- Geographical dispersion. Top 10 state risk-in-force concentration was about average for the industry.
Concentration in California was moderately high at 20.8% of risk as of Dec. 31, 1996 (industry 17.1%), although the company is aggressively reducing California exposure.

-- Nonconforming business. United Guaranty Residential Insurance writes a very restricted amount of pool insurance of 'A'-quality mortgages which are individually too big to conform to the requirements of the "government-sponsored enterprises" and are known as "non-conforming" mortgages.
It also underwrites a larger share of primary insurance for these loans than the industry. The mortgages tend to be geographically concentrated in California.

In the past, this type of pool insurance has produced heavy losses for mortgage insurers other than United Guaranty Residential Insurance which were much more exposed to the risk produced by the product than the company.

-- Increasing loss ratios. At 49.1%, United Guaranty Residential Insurance's loss ratio was the highest of the past five years. It is nominally better than the industry's 49.7%, but the industry's loss ratio is skewed by heavy non-conforming pool losses sustained by other mortgage insurers.
The ratio itself is good.
Expectations:

Assuming continued strength in the U.S. economy without the development of new pockets of recession, Standard & Poor's anticipates earnings growth will still slow in 1997 and plateau or decline in 1998 for United Guaranty Residential Insurance and the industry as a whole for several reasons:
-- The move into peak loss years of the large 1992 and 1993 books of business;
-- Declining first-year premium compared to 1995 and 1996 as the 1997 purchase market will be slightly off from 1996 and refinance business at this writing (June, 1997) looks weak;
-- More than acceptable but still relatively weak performance compared to the preceding five prior years of the 1994 to 1996 books;
-- Higher average loan to value ratios of new mortgages insured; and

-- Increasing competition in the industry. United Guaranty Residential Insurance will largely offset these negatives by renewal volume from recent high-volume years; the favorable statutory accounting effect in the early years of new business which generates high premiums due to deeper coverage requirements imposed by the "government-sponsored enterprises"; and decent performance of the overall book.
